r: A share of ownership in a corporation
Stockholders own part of the company.
w: A loan that a company repays with fixed interest over time
That describes a bond.
A certificate that guarantees a company will never lose money for its investors
Stocks carry risk.
A contract that gives a person the right to run the daily business of a firm
Ownership is not management.

r: A loan made by an investor to a company or government
The issuer promises to repay with interest.
w: A share of ownership that gives the holder a vote at the annual meeting
That describes common stock.
A savings account that a bank insures up to a legal limit for each depositor
That describes a bank deposit.
A contract that lets the holder buy shares at a set price before a given date
That describes an option.

r: A payment a company makes to shareholders from its profits
Dividends are set by the board of directors.
w: A fee that a broker charges each time a client buys or sells a security
That is a commission.
The interest that a bond issuer pays on money borrowed from investors
That is a coupon payment.
A tax that the government charges on gains from selling shares of stock
That is a capital gains tax.

r: A pool of money from many investors used to buy a mix of securities
A manager invests the pooled money.
w: A single stock that is owned jointly by two or more friends or relatives
A fund holds many securities, not one.
A bank account that pays a fixed rate of interest and is insured by the FDIC
That is a certificate of deposit or savings.
A loan that a group of investors makes to a single company to build a new plant
That is a private loan.

r: A basket of securities that trades on an exchange like a single stock
Its price changes throughout the trading day.
w: A fund that can be bought or sold only once a day after the market closes
That describes a traditional mutual fund.
A savings plan that an employer sets up to pay for a worker's retirement
That describes a retirement plan.
A loan that a bank gives to a company that wants to sell its goods overseas
That is trade finance.

q: What is the main difference between common and preferred stock?
r: Preferred stock usually pays a fixed dividend and ranks ahead of common in payouts
Common stock usually carries voting rights.
w: Common stock always pays a fixed dividend while preferred stock never pays any dividend at all
The reverse is closer to the truth.
Preferred stock gives holders the right to vote on every decision made by the board of directors
Common stock usually carries the votes.
Common stock can be bought only by large institutions while preferred stock is sold to the public
Both can be bought by individuals.

r: A short-term U.S. government debt security sold at a discount
It matures in a year or less.
w: A long-term corporate bond that pays interest twice a year for thirty years
Treasury bills are short term.
A share of stock in the Treasury Department that pays a dividend to its holders
The government has no stock.
A bank deposit that is insured by the FDIC and pays a fixed rate for five years
That is a certificate of deposit.

q: What is a coupon rate on a bond?
r: The annual interest rate paid on the bond's face value
It is usually fixed when the bond is issued.
w: The price at which the bond trades in the market on any given day of the year
That is the market price.
The total return an investor earns if the bond is held until it matures in full
That is yield to maturity.
The fee a broker charges for helping an investor buy the bond from the issuer
That is a commission.

q: What is the face (par) value of a bond?
r: The amount the issuer repays the holder when the bond matures
Often $1,000 per bond.
w: The price at which the bond is bought and sold among investors in the market
That is the market price.
The yearly interest payment the issuer makes to the person who holds the bond
That is the coupon payment.
The amount of tax an investor owes on the interest earned from the bond each year
That is a tax amount.

q: What happens to bond prices when interest rates rise?
r: Existing bond prices generally fall
New bonds pay more, so older ones lose appeal.
w: Existing bond prices generally rise because their older rates look more attractive to buyers
The opposite happens.
Bond prices stay exactly the same because the face value of each bond is fixed by law
Market prices move with rates.
Bond prices double in value because the government guarantees a gain when rates go up
No such guarantee exists.

r: A bond issued by a state or local government
Interest is often exempt from federal income tax.
w: A bond issued by the federal government to pay for national defense and highways
That is a Treasury bond.
A bond issued by a foreign corporation to raise money for projects in other countries
That is a foreign corporate bond.
A bond that pays no interest and is sold by a bank to depositors at a deep discount
That describes a zero-coupon bond.

r: A bond sold at a discount that pays no periodic interest
The holder is paid face value at maturity.
w: A bond that pays interest every month and returns less than face value at maturity
Zero-coupon bonds pay no interest.
A bond that can be traded only after the holder has paid a coupon to the issuer
No such rule exists.
A bond that pays a higher rate of interest than any other bond in the market
It pays no periodic interest.

q: What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?
r: A deposit held for a fixed term at a fixed rate, usually insured by the FDIC
Early withdrawal often brings a penalty.
w: A stock that pays a high dividend and can be sold on an exchange at any time
A CD is a bank product.
A bond issued by a company that promises to repay holders after exactly ten years
A CD is a deposit, not a bond.
A checking account that lets the owner write checks without paying any bank fees
A CD locks in the money for a term.

q: What is a money market fund?
r: A mutual fund that invests in short-term, low-risk debt
It aims to keep a stable share price.
w: A fund that invests only in new companies hoping for very large gains in value
That is a risky growth fund.
A fund that buys real estate and rents it out to tenants to earn income
That is a real estate fund.
A fund that holds only shares of one large company and follows its stock price
That is a single-stock fund.

r: A fund that aims to match the performance of a market index
It holds the securities in the index.
w: A fund whose manager tries to beat the market by picking only the very best stocks
That is an actively managed fund.
A fund that invests only in bonds issued by cities and towns across the country
That is a municipal bond fund.
A fund that lends money to investors who want to buy shares on credit from a broker
That is margin lending.

r: A contract giving the holder the right to buy a security at a set price
The holder is not obliged to buy.
w: A contract giving the holder the right to sell a security at a set price before a date
That describes a put option.
A contract that obliges the holder to buy a security at a set price on a set date
An option gives a right, not an obligation.
A phone call a broker makes to a client to suggest a new stock for purchase
That is not an option contract.

r: A contract giving the holder the right to sell a security at a set price
The holder is not obliged to sell.
w: A contract giving the holder the right to buy a security at a set price before a date
That describes a call option.
A contract that obliges the holder to sell a security at a set price on a set date
An option gives a right, not an obligation.
A request to the broker to place an order for a stock at the opening of the market
That is an order, not an option.

r: A financial contract whose value depends on an underlying asset
Options and futures are examples.
w: A share of ownership in a company that pays a dividend out of its yearly profits
That is a stock.
A loan made by an investor to a government that pays interest every six months
That is a bond.
A deposit in a bank that earns a fixed rate of interest for a set number of years
That is a certificate of deposit.

r: An agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date
Both sides are obliged to complete the deal.
w: A right, but not an obligation, to buy a stock at a price chosen by the holder
That describes an option.
A bond that pays interest for the next thirty years to the person who holds it
That is a long-term bond.
A forecast made by an analyst about how a stock will perform in the next year
That is an estimate, not a contract.

q: What is a real estate investment trust (REIT)?
r: A company that owns or finances income-producing real estate and pays out most income
Investors buy shares like stock.
w: A bank loan used by a family to purchase a home with a fixed rate for thirty years
That is a mortgage.
A government agency that sets the rent that landlords may charge for apartments
A REIT is not an agency.
A fund that invests only in gold and other precious metals held in a vault
That is a commodity fund.

q: What is an American Depositary Receipt (ADR)?
r: A certificate that lets U.S. investors trade shares of a foreign company
ADRs trade on U.S. exchanges.
w: A loan from an American bank to a foreign firm that wishes to build a plant in the U.S.
An ADR is not a loan.
A tax form that foreign investors must file when they buy shares in a U.S. company
An ADR is a security, not a form.
A government bond sold by the U.S. Treasury to investors who live in other countries
That is a Treasury bond.

r: A company increases its shares outstanding and lowers the price per share
Total value stays the same.
w: A company pays out half of its yearly profits to shareholders as a cash dividend
That is a dividend.
A company sells half of its shares to the public to raise money for a new project
That is a stock offering.
A company's stock falls by half because of bad news about its future earnings
A split is a planned change.

r: A company repurchases its own shares from investors
It reduces the number of shares outstanding.
w: A company sells new shares to investors to raise money for building a second plant
That is a stock offering.
An investor returns shares to a broker and receives a full refund of what was paid
Buybacks are done by the company.
A company gives its shareholders extra shares in place of paying a cash dividend
That is a stock dividend.

r: A stock of a large, well-established company with a record of reliable earnings
These firms are seen as lower risk.
w: A stock of a small new company with no profits that is expected to grow very fast
That is a speculative growth stock.
A stock that sells for less than one dollar a share and trades outside the main exchanges
That is a penny stock.
A stock that pays no dividends and whose price changes sharply from one week to the next
That does not define blue chips.

r: A stock of a company expected to grow faster than the overall market
It often reinvests profits rather than paying dividends.
w: A stock of a mature company that pays large steady dividends and rarely changes in price
That describes an income stock.
A stock that is priced far below the value of the assets the company holds on its books
That describes a value stock.
A stock that is sold only to the employees of the company that issued the shares
That is an employee stock plan.

r: A stock that appears to trade below its true worth
Investors hope the price will rise.
w: A stock that trades at a very high price compared with its earnings and its assets
That suggests overvaluation.
A stock that is expected to grow faster than any other stock in the market this year
That describes a growth stock.
A stock that is guaranteed by the government to rise in value every single year
No stock is guaranteed.

r: A stock of a company with a very large market value
Market cap is shares times price.
w: A stock of a company with a very small market value that trades in thin markets
That is a small-cap stock.
A stock whose price is above one hundred dollars per share on the exchange today
Price per share does not set the cap.
A stock that only large banks and insurance companies are allowed to buy and hold
Individuals can buy large caps.

r: The market where new securities are first sold by the issuer
The issuer receives the money raised.
w: The market where investors buy and sell securities among themselves after they are issued
That is the secondary market.
The market where only government bonds are traded between large banks overnight
That is part of the bond market.
The market where goods are bought and sold directly between two private persons
That is a private sale.

r: The market where investors trade securities that were already issued
The issuer receives no money from these trades.
w: The market where new securities are sold for the first time by the company that issues them
That is the primary market.
The market where companies sell their goods to other companies at a wholesale price
That is a wholesale market.
The market where only the smallest firms are allowed to list their shares for sale
No such rule defines it.

q: What is an initial public offering (IPO)?
r: A company's first sale of shares to the public
It moves a firm from private to public ownership.
w: A company's purchase of its own shares from the investors who currently hold them
That is a buyback.
A company's sale of bonds to a single bank to raise money for a short period
That is a private loan.
A company's decision to pay out half of its profits to shareholders each year
That is a dividend policy.

q: What does an underwriter do in an IPO?
r: Helps the company price and sell its new shares to investors
It often takes on some of the risk.
w: Writes the insurance policies that protect the company against any loss of its factories
That is an insurer.
Audits the financial statements of the firm and signs a report for the stockholders
That is an auditor.
Votes on behalf of the shareholders at the annual meeting of the corporation
That is a proxy holder.

r: A marketplace where securities are bought and sold
Examples include the NYSE and Nasdaq.
w: A government agency that sets the price of each share traded on a given business day
Prices are set by supply and demand.
A bank that lends money to investors who wish to buy shares of stock on credit
That is a margin lender.
A firm that prepares the tax returns of public companies for the federal government
That is an accounting firm.

q: What is the Dow Jones Industrial Average?
r: A price-weighted index of 30 large U.S. companies
It is a common gauge of the market.
w: A market-cap-weighted index of 500 large companies from many different industries
That describes the S&P 500.
An index of thousands of small companies listed on exchanges in the United States
That describes a broader index.
A list of the thirty bonds with the highest yields that are sold in a given year
It tracks stocks, not bonds.

r: A market-cap-weighted index of 500 large U.S. companies
It is widely used as a benchmark.
w: A price-weighted index of 30 large companies that are chosen by the editors of a newspaper
That describes the Dow.
An index that tracks only the stocks of small technology firms listed on Nasdaq
That is a narrower index.
A government fund that invests in the 500 largest banks of the United States
It is an index, not a fund.

r: Listing many technology and growth companies on an electronic exchange
It has no traditional trading floor.
w: Being the oldest trading floor in the world where traders shout orders in a crowd
That describes the NYSE image.
Trading only government bonds and other debt among the largest banks in the country
Nasdaq lists stocks.
Setting the interest rates that banks charge each other on loans made overnight
That is the Federal Reserve's role.

r: A period when prices are rising or expected to rise
Investor confidence is high.
w: A period when prices fall sharply, often by 20 percent or more, for several months
That is a bear market.
A period when the exchanges are closed for a holiday and no trading takes place
That is a market closure.
A period when prices stay almost the same for several years and trading is thin
That is a flat market.

r: A period of generally falling prices, often 20 percent or more
Investor pessimism is high.
w: A period when prices are rising and investors expect them to keep rising for years
That is a bull market.
A period when the government buys stocks to keep prices from falling any further
That is an intervention.
A period when trading volume is at its highest level of the year in all markets
Volume does not define it.

r: The total market value of a company's outstanding shares
Share price times shares outstanding.
w: The total amount of cash that a company has in its bank accounts at the end of the year
That is a cash balance.
The total amount a company owes to banks and bondholders at a given point in time
That is debt.
The amount a company pays to its shareholders in dividends over a full fiscal year
That is total dividends.

r: How quickly an asset can be sold for cash without a big price drop
Stocks of large firms are very liquid.
w: How much interest an asset pays to its owner over the span of a calendar year
That is yield.
How much the price of an asset moves up and down in a given period of trading
That is volatility.
How many shares of a company the investor is allowed to hold at the same time
That is an ownership limit.

r: How much and how quickly the price of an asset moves up and down
Higher volatility means more risk.
w: How easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing much of its value
That is liquidity.
How much interest or dividend income an asset pays out to its owner each year
That is yield.
How long an investor plans to hold an asset before selling it for a profit
That is a time horizon.

q: What is a circuit breaker on an exchange?
r: A rule that pauses trading when prices fall by a set amount
It gives investors time to react.
w: A device that cuts the electricity to the trading floor in case of a fire in the building
It is a trading rule.
A fee that is charged to traders who buy and sell too many shares within one day
It is a pause, not a fee.
A rule that bans short sales for the first hour of every trading session of the week
That is a different rule.

r: The highest price a buyer is willing to pay for a security
It is what a seller receives when selling.
w: The lowest price a seller is willing to accept for a security at that moment in the market
That is the ask price.
The average price of a security over the past twelve months of trading on an exchange
That is an average.
The price at which a security was first offered to the public by the company that issued it
That is an offering price.

r: The lowest price a seller is willing to accept for a security
It is what a buyer pays when buying.
w: The highest price a buyer is willing to pay for a security at that moment in the market
That is the bid price.
The price that the broker charges the client for placing the order on an exchange
That is a commission.
The closing price of a security on the last trading day of the calendar year
That is a closing price.

r: The difference between the highest bid and the lowest ask
A narrow spread signals a liquid market.
w: The difference between a stock's price at the start of the year and at the end
That is the annual change.
The fee a broker charges for buying or selling a security on behalf of a client
That is a commission.
The gap between the interest rate on a bond and the rate of inflation in the economy
That is a real rate.

q: What does a market maker do?
r: Stands ready to buy and sell a security to keep trading smooth
It earns the spread between bid and ask.
w: Decides which companies are allowed to list their shares on a given stock exchange
That is a listing committee.
Sets the interest rate that banks charge each other on loans made overnight
That is the central bank.
Prepares the audited statements that public companies must file with the regulator
That is an auditor.

r: An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price
Execution is fast but the price is not fixed.
w: An order to buy or sell only at a specific price or a better one chosen by the investor
That is a limit order.
An order to sell a stock if its price falls to a level that the investor has chosen
That is a stop order.
An order that stays open for one full year until the investor decides to cancel it
That is a time-in-force setting.

r: An order to buy or sell at a specified price or better
It may not be filled if the price is not reached.
w: An order to buy or sell immediately at the best price that is available in the market
That is a market order.
An order that limits the number of shares an investor may own in a single company
No such order exists.
An order that is carried out only by the broker's own staff and never by a computer
The method does not define it.

r: An order to sell when a price falls to a set level
It helps limit losses.
w: An order to buy a stock when the price rises above a level chosen by the investor
That is a buy-stop order.
An order that prevents a broker from selling any shares for a period of thirty days
That is not a stop-loss order.
An order to buy a stock at the lowest price of the year however long it takes
No such order exists.

r: Selling borrowed shares hoping to buy them back at a lower price
Losses can be unlimited if the price rises.
w: Selling shares that you own within one year of buying them to lock in a small gain
That is a short-term sale.
Selling shares only for a very brief time during the opening minutes of trading
Duration of the trade is not the idea.
Buying a small number of shares of many companies to spread risk across industries
That is diversification.

r: Borrowing money from a broker to buy securities
It magnifies both gains and losses.
w: Trading only shares of companies that are listed in the margin of a financial newspaper
That is not margin trading.
Buying securities using only the investor's own cash with no borrowing at all
That is a cash purchase.
Trading at the edges of the market where prices change by the smallest possible amount
That is not margin trading.

r: A broker's demand for more money when account value falls too far
The investor must deposit funds or sell assets.
w: A phone call from a broker offering a bonus to clients who open a new margin account
That is a sales call.
A notice that tells the investor a stock has reached the price chosen for a limit order
That is an order confirmation.
A request from the exchange for a company to explain a sudden change in its share price
That is an exchange inquiry.

r: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price
It can lower the average cost per share.
w: Investing the whole sum at once on the day when the market reaches its highest point
That is lump-sum investing at a peak.
Waiting for the lowest price of the year before making any purchase of shares at all
That is market timing.
Buying only shares that cost exactly one dollar each on the exchange
Price per share is not the idea.

r: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk
It avoids putting all eggs in one basket.
w: Putting all of your money into the one stock that you think will grow the most
That concentrates risk.
Selling all of your investments when prices fall and holding only cash for a long time
That is moving to cash.
Buying only the shares of companies that are located in the same industry and region
That concentrates risk.

r: Market-wide risk that cannot be removed by diversification
Recessions are an example.
w: Risk that is unique to one company or industry and can be reduced by diversification
That is unsystematic risk.
Risk that arises only when an investor borrows money from a broker to buy shares
That is leverage risk.
Risk that a bond issuer fails to make interest payments on the date they are due
That is credit risk.

r: The risk that a borrower fails to repay interest or principal
Bond ratings measure it.
w: The risk that rising prices reduce the buying power of the returns earned on an asset
That is inflation risk.
The risk that an asset cannot be sold quickly without accepting a lower price
That is liquidity risk.
The risk that market interest rates rise and cause existing bond prices to fall
That is interest rate risk.

r: The risk that rising prices erode the buying power of returns
Fixed payments lose real value.
w: The risk that a company fails and cannot repay the money it borrowed from bondholders
That is credit risk.
The risk that an investor cannot find a buyer for a security when needing cash
That is liquidity risk.
The risk that the government changes the rules about how investment gains are taxed
That is regulatory risk.

q: What is interest rate risk for bond investors?
r: The risk that rising rates reduce the market price of existing bonds
Longer maturities are more sensitive.
w: The risk that a company will skip a dividend payment because profits were lower than hoped
That is dividend risk.
The risk that a bond is repaid early so the investor must reinvest at lower rates
That is call or prepayment risk.
The risk that a bond issuer will change its name and the investor cannot find the holding
That is not a defined risk.

q: What does the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compare?
r: A stock's price with the company's earnings per share
A higher ratio can suggest growth expectations.
w: A stock's price with the total value of the assets owned by the company at book value
That is price to book.
A company's total debt with the total value of the equity held by its owners
That is debt to equity.
A stock's dividend with the price of one share on the market
That is dividend yield.

r: Net income divided by the number of shares outstanding
It shows profit attributed to each share.
w: The total revenue of a company divided by the number of its employees on payroll
That is revenue per employee.
The price of one share of stock divided by the dividend paid in the last year
That is a payout measure.
The total assets of a company divided by the number of its outstanding bonds
That is not EPS.

r: Annual dividends per share divided by the share price
It shows income relative to price.
w: The price of one share divided by the earnings per share over the last twelve months
That is the P/E ratio.
The total profit of the company divided by the number of shares held by its employees
That is not dividend yield.
The growth in a stock's price over a year divided by its price at the start of the year
That is price return.

q: What is the dividend payout ratio?
r: The share of earnings paid out to shareholders as dividends
A low ratio means more profit is retained.
w: The share price of a stock divided by its earnings per share over the past year
That is the P/E ratio.
The annual dividend divided by the market price of one share at the current date
That is dividend yield.
The total debt of the company divided by the equity that its owners have invested
That is leverage.

r: Net income divided by shareholders' equity
It shows profit earned on owners' investment.
w: Net income divided by total sales for the year, shown as a percent of revenue
That is net profit margin.
Total assets divided by total liabilities of the company at the end of the period
That is a solvency ratio.
Annual dividends divided by the market price of one share of the company's stock
That is dividend yield.

r: Net income divided by average total assets
It shows how efficiently assets earn profit.
w: Net income divided by shareholders' equity at the end of the fiscal year in dollars
That is return on equity.
Total revenue divided by the number of workers employed by the company that year
That is revenue per employee.
Total debt divided by total assets owned by the business on the balance sheet date
That is the debt ratio.

r: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity
It shows how much a firm relies on borrowing.
w: Net income divided by total sales for the year, expressed as a percentage of revenue
That is profit margin.
Current assets divided by current liabilities of the company at the balance sheet date
That is the current ratio.
The share price divided by the earnings per share of the company for one year
That is the P/E ratio.

q: What does the current ratio measure?
r: A firm's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets
Current assets divided by current liabilities.
w: A firm's total debt compared with the equity that its shareholders have invested
That is the debt-to-equity ratio.
A firm's profit compared with its total sales over the fiscal year in percent
That is profit margin.
A firm's stock price compared with its earnings for each share held by investors
That is the P/E ratio.

q: What does a stock's beta measure?
r: How much the stock moves relative to the overall market
A beta above 1 means more volatile than the market.
w: How much dividend income the stock pays to investors compared with its price each year
That is yield.
How much profit the company earns on each dollar of its sales during the year
That is margin.
How many shares of the stock are traded on the exchange on an average day
That is trading volume.

r: Judging a security's value by studying financial statements and the economy
It looks for the intrinsic value.
w: Predicting prices by studying charts of past prices and trading volume for patterns
That is technical analysis.
Choosing stocks by following the advice of friends and relatives who invest regularly
That is a tip-based approach.
Buying whichever stock has risen the most during the past week without further study
That is momentum chasing.

r: Studying price charts and trading volume to forecast prices
It assumes patterns tend to repeat.
w: Judging a security's value by studying financial statements and the state of the economy
That is fundamental analysis.
Interviewing the managers of a company to learn about its plans for new products
That is qualitative research.
Reading the annual report to learn which assets the company holds on its balance sheet
That is a part of fundamental analysis.

r: The estimated true worth of an asset based on fundamentals
It may differ from the market price.
w: The price at which an asset currently trades on an exchange between buyers and sellers
That is the market price.
The price an investor originally paid when buying the asset, including all fees
That is the cost basis.
The value of an asset as shown in a dealer's advertisement or on a stock certificate
That is not intrinsic value.

q: What is book value per share?
r: Shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding
It shows accounting value per share.
w: The price at which a share last traded on the exchange before the market closed
That is the market price.
Annual earnings of the company divided by the number of employees on its payroll
That is not book value.
Total debt of the company divided by the number of shares that it has issued
That is not book value.

r: The total return on a bond held until it matures
It accounts for price, coupon and time.
w: The annual interest rate paid on the face value of the bond by the issuer
That is the coupon rate.
The current price at which the bond trades in the market on the day it is quoted
That is the market price.
The amount repaid to the holder when the bond reaches its maturity date
That is the face value.

r: An assessment of the issuer's ability to repay its debt
Agencies like Moody's and S&P assign them.
w: The interest rate set by the Federal Reserve for all bonds sold in the market this year
Ratings come from agencies.
A ranking of bonds by how many investors have bought them in the last month
Ratings are not popularity.
A tax code assigned to each bond by the revenue agency for the use of the issuer
That is not a rating.

r: A bond with a low credit rating that pays higher interest
The higher yield compensates for default risk.
w: A bond issued by the U.S. government that is backed by the full faith of the Treasury
That is a Treasury bond.
A bond with the highest credit rating that pays the lowest interest of any issue
That is investment grade.
A bond that has already matured and can no longer be sold to any other investors
That is a matured bond.

r: A shortcut to estimate how long money takes to double
Divide 72 by the annual rate of return.
w: A rule that says investors must retire from work when they reach the age of seventy-two
Not a retirement rule.
A rule that limits the number of trades an investor may place in a single day to seventy-two
No such limit exists.
A rule that sets the maximum interest a bank may charge at seventy-two percent a year
No such cap exists.

q: What is compound growth in investing?
r: Earnings that generate their own earnings over time
Reinvested returns speed up growth.
w: Earnings that are spent immediately so that nothing remains invested for the future
That removes compounding.
Earnings that are paid only on the original amount invested and never on past interest
That is simple interest.
Earnings that are guaranteed by the government to rise by a fixed amount each year
No such guarantee exists.

r: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
Safer assets tend to pay less.
w: Higher potential returns always come with no risk at all for the careful investor
Return requires risk.
Lower risk always produces higher returns for the investor who buys the safest assets
Safer assets pay less.
Risk and return are completely unrelated so that one says nothing about the other
They are linked.

r: Dividing a portfolio among asset classes such as stocks, bonds and cash
It is a key driver of risk and return.
w: Putting the whole portfolio into one stock that the investor expects to rise the fastest
That is concentration.
Selling every holding at once and moving all money into a savings account at a bank
That is liquidating.
Choosing the broker who charges the lowest commissions on trades for a given year
That is picking a broker.

r: Adjusting holdings back to target allocations
It keeps risk in line with the plan.
w: Selling the whole portfolio and starting again with a new set of investments
That is liquidating.
Buying more of the asset that has risen the most in the past year to follow the trend
That is momentum chasing.
Moving all money into cash whenever the stock market falls by more than ten percent
That is market timing.

r: How long an investor expects to hold investments before needing the money
A longer horizon can support more risk.
w: The number of hours the stock market is open for trading on a normal business day
That is trading hours.
The date on which a company must report its earnings to the public each quarter
That is a reporting date.
The period during which an investor may cancel a trade after placing the order
That is a cancellation window.

r: How much loss in value an investor can accept without panic
It depends on goals and temperament.
w: How much an investor earns from a job in a year, before taxes and any deductions
That is income.
How much interest a bank pays on a savings account in the course of a year
That is a rate.
How many different stocks an investor holds in a portfolio at a single moment
That is portfolio size.

r: The yearly fee a fund charges as a percent of assets
It reduces investor returns.
w: The commission a broker charges when an investor buys or sells shares in a fund
That is a trading commission.
The share of a fund's profit that is paid out to investors as a distribution
That is a payout.
The tax that an investor pays on gains made from selling shares of a fund
That is a tax.

q: What is a load on a mutual fund?
r: A sales charge paid when buying or selling fund shares
No-load funds have none.
w: The weight of the securities that a mutual fund holds in its portfolio at year end
Not a measure of weight.
The amount of debt that a fund has taken on to buy securities for its investors
That is leverage.
The yearly fee a fund charges to cover management and operating costs for investors
That is the expense ratio.

q: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) do?
r: Regulates securities markets to protect investors
It enforces federal securities laws.
w: Sets the interest rates that banks charge one another on loans made for one night
That is the Federal Reserve.
Collects income taxes from individuals and businesses throughout the United States
That is the IRS.
Insures bank deposits up to a legal limit in case a bank fails
That is the FDIC.

r: A self-regulatory organization that oversees brokerage firms and brokers
It licenses and examines brokers.
w: A stock exchange where shares of large companies are bought and sold every day
FINRA is not an exchange.
A federal agency that sets the interest rate on loans to home buyers across the nation
That is not FINRA.
A credit rating agency that grades the debt of corporations and governments
That is a rating agency.

r: A nonprofit that protects customers if a brokerage firm fails
It does not cover market losses.
w: A federal agency that insures bank deposits up to a legal limit for each depositor
That is the FDIC.
A government fund that guarantees investors against any loss in the value of their stocks
SIPC covers broker failure only.
A stock exchange that lists the shares of small and mid-sized companies for trade
SIPC is not an exchange.

r: Deposits in insured banks up to the legal limit
It does not cover stocks or bonds.
w: Stocks and bonds that are bought through a bank and held in an investment account
These are not insured by the FDIC.
Losses an investor suffers when the stock market falls over a period of several months
Market losses are not covered.
Money held in a brokerage account if the broker goes out of business with a loss
That is SIPC.

r: A broker who gives advice and research as well as executing trades
It usually charges higher fees.
w: A broker who only executes orders for clients and offers no advice or research reports
That is a discount broker.
A broker who works for only one company and may sell only that company's own shares
That is a captive broker.
A computer program that picks investments for clients and charges a very low yearly fee
That is a robo-advisor.

r: A broker who executes trades at low cost with little or no advice
Clients make their own decisions.
w: A broker who gives personal advice and in-depth research to clients for a large fee
That is a full-service broker.
A broker who sells only securities that are being offered at a deep discount to price
That is not the definition.
A broker who works for free and is paid only by the companies whose shares are sold
Brokers earn fees or commissions.

r: An automated service that manages portfolios using algorithms
Fees are usually lower than for human advisers.
w: A human financial planner who meets clients in person to discuss their goals each year
That is a human adviser.
A machine that prints stock certificates for the clients of a brokerage firm each day
That is not a robo-advisor.
A robot that works on the floor of the exchange and shouts orders to other traders
That is not what the term means.

r: A professional legally required to act in a client's best interest
It is a higher standard than suitability.
w: A person who sells investments and may recommend any product that earns the most commission
That is not a fiduciary duty.
A person who keeps the records of a company and prepares its yearly financial statements
That is an accountant.
A person who invests only the money of his own family and has no clients at all
That is a private investor.

r: Recommendations must fit the client's profile and goals
Brokers must have reasonable grounds.
w: Brokers may recommend any security that earns them the highest commission on each sale
That would ignore the client.
Clients must be suitable for the broker, meaning they have to hold a certain amount of cash
The rule protects clients.
Brokers must recommend only the safest bonds to every client regardless of their goals
Recommendations must fit the client.

r: Trading securities using material nonpublic information
It is illegal and enforced by the SEC.
w: Trading securities on the floor of the exchange by members who work inside the building
Location is not the issue.
Trading securities that were bought through a company's own employee stock plan
That is a legal plan.
Trading securities in a retirement account that is managed by a company's own staff
That is a retirement account.

r: A fraud that pays earlier investors with money from newer investors
It collapses when new money dries up.
w: A legal plan in which a company pays its shareholders a dividend from its own profit
That is a normal dividend.
A government bond program that pays a fixed interest rate to citizens who save money
That is a savings bond.
A retirement plan in which an employer matches what a worker puts into the account
That is a retirement match.

q: Which is a red flag of investment fraud?
r: Promises of guaranteed high returns with little or no risk
Real investments carry risk.
w: A registered adviser who explains the risks of an investment and shows a public record
That is a sign of legitimacy.
A clear written prospectus that describes the fees, goals and risks of a fund in detail
That is a sign of legitimacy.
A broker who asks about the client's goals and income before suggesting any purchase
That is good practice.

r: A document describing an investment's goals, fees and risks
Investors should read it before buying.
w: A list of the names of the brokers who work at a given firm along with their phone numbers
It is not a staff list.
A report that shows the price of each stock traded on the exchange on the previous day
That is a price list.
A tax form that investors file each year to report the gains made on their securities
That is a tax form.

q: What does the Securities Act of 1933 mainly require?
r: Disclosure when securities are first sold to the public
It protects investors in new issues.
w: Regulation of trading on exchanges after securities have already been issued to investors
That is the 1934 Act.
A limit on the interest rates that banks can charge their customers on home loans
That is not its purpose.
Insurance of bank deposits up to a limit for each person who holds an account
That is the FDIC.

q: What does the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 do?
r: Regulates trading of securities and created the SEC
It covers the secondary market.
w: Requires disclosure when securities are first sold to the public by an issuer
That is the 1933 Act.
Sets the rate of tax that investors must pay on gains from selling securities
That is tax law.
Limits the amount of interest that banks may pay on the deposits of their customers
That is not its purpose.

q: What did the Sarbanes-Oxley Act mainly address?
r: Accuracy and honesty in financial reporting by public companies
It followed major accounting scandals.
w: Limits on imports from other countries and the tariffs charged at the ports of entry
It is not a trade law.
The rules for how banks may lend money to home buyers who have poor credit histories
That is mortgage regulation.
The minimum wage that must be paid to workers in all states of the country
That is labor law.

q: What is a custodian in the securities industry?
r: An institution that holds and safeguards investors' securities
It keeps assets separate from the broker's own.
w: A person who buys stock for the government and holds it in a vault at the central bank
Not a government role.
A trader on the floor of an exchange who shouts orders to other traders all day
Not a custodian.
A manager who decides which stocks a mutual fund will buy for its portfolio
That is a portfolio manager.

q: What does clearing and settlement mean?
r: Completing a trade so ownership and money change hands
It follows the execution of an order.
w: The process of printing statements and mailing them to customers at the end of each month
That is reporting.
The process of checking that a company's financial statements were prepared correctly
That is an audit.
The process of listing a new company's shares for the first time on an exchange
That is a listing.

r: Rules requiring firms to verify clients' identity and profile
They help prevent fraud and money laundering.
w: A rule requiring customers to know the broker's salary before they open an account
No such rule exists.
A rule that lets brokers share a client's private data with any company that asks for it
That would violate privacy.
A rule that sets the minimum amount a customer must deposit to start trading
That is an account minimum.

r: Hiding the origin of illegally obtained money by making it look legitimate
Financial firms must watch for it.
w: Washing banknotes in a machine to remove dirt before they are returned to circulation
That is literal cleaning.
Moving money between two accounts held by the same person at a single bank branch
That is a transfer.
Paying taxes on income earned abroad in the country where the money was earned
That is tax compliance.

q: Which investment is generally best for a short-term goal in one year?
r: A savings account or short-term CD
They protect principal and are easy to reach.
w: A single speculative stock that may rise or fall sharply within the next twelve months
Too risky for a near goal.
A twenty-year corporate bond whose price can swing widely when interest rates change
Too sensitive to rates.
A fund that invests only in new technology firms with no profits and large price swings
Too risky for a near goal.

q: Why does a longer time horizon usually allow for more risk?
r: There is more time to recover from market dips
Stocks have historically recovered over long periods.
w: Investments cannot lose value when they are held for more than five years in a row
Losses can still occur.
Fees disappear after the first year so the investor pays nothing more to the fund company
Fees continue.
Banks guarantee a profit to every investor who holds a stock for more than a decade
No such guarantee exists.

q: Which investor would most likely hold a higher share of stocks?
r: A 25-year-old saving for retirement in 40 years
A long horizon can absorb dips.
w: A retiree who needs the money next month to pay for living costs and medical bills
A short horizon needs safety.
A family saving for a house payment that is due in six months from this date
A short horizon needs safety.
A person who cannot accept any loss in value of savings under any circumstances
A low tolerance needs safety.

q: What does it mean to be a conservative investor?
r: Prioritizing safety of principal over high returns
Prefers bonds, cash and stable assets.
w: Seeking the highest possible returns even if it means accepting large losses along the way
That is aggressive.
Buying and selling stocks every day to profit from small changes in price
That is day trading.
Putting all savings into one new company that the investor thinks will become a leader
That is concentrated speculation.

q: What does it mean to be an aggressive investor?
r: Accepting more risk for higher potential return
Holds a larger share of stocks.
w: Prioritizing safety of principal over high returns and avoiding stocks wherever possible
That is conservative.
Keeping all savings in a bank account that is insured by the federal government
That is very conservative.
Buying only government bonds that mature within one year and pay a small fixed rate
That is very conservative.

q: Why are index funds popular with long-term investors?
r: They offer broad diversification at low cost
Fees are usually small.
w: They guarantee that the investor will earn more than the market in every single year
No such guarantee exists.
They remove all risk of loss because the government insures the value of each share
They carry market risk.
They are available only to wealthy investors who can place very large orders at once
Anyone can buy them.

q: Why can high fees hurt long-term returns?
r: They reduce the amount that stays invested and compounds
Small yearly costs add up over decades.
w: They have no effect after the first year because they are charged only a single time
Fees are charged yearly.
They increase the return of the fund because the manager works harder for higher pay
Fees do not raise returns.
They are refunded to investors each year by the fund company in the form of a rebate
Fees are not refunded.

q: Which is a reason to avoid holding too much of your employer's stock?
r: Your job and your investments depend on the same company
A downturn could hit both at once.
w: Employer stock cannot lose value because the company's managers control the share price
It can lose value.
Employees are legally banned from selling their company's stock for five years
No such ban applies to all.
Employer stock always pays a lower dividend than any other kind of stock available
Dividends vary.

r: A fund that shifts toward safer assets as a retirement date nears
It adjusts the mix automatically.
w: A fund that pays out all of its assets on one set date to the investors who hold it
It does not liquidate on that date.
A fund that invests only in companies that are planning to go public in the next year
That is an IPO fund.
A fund that buys stocks only on the last trading day of the month for each client
That is not a target-date fund.

r: A fund that holds a mix of stocks and bonds
It aims to blend growth and income.
w: A fund that holds only stocks of one industry and follows a single narrow theme
That is a sector fund.
A fund that holds only cash and short-term government debt to protect principal
That is a money market fund.
A fund that is balanced by order of the government so that no investor loses money
No such order exists.

q: What is the main benefit of an employer 401(k) match?
r: It adds free money based on what the employee contributes
It boosts retirement savings.
w: It lets the employee withdraw the money at any time without tax or penalty of any kind
Early withdrawals are restricted.
It guarantees that the investments in the account will never lose any value over time
Investments can lose value.
It removes the need for the employee to pay any income tax on wages in the year
Wages are still taxed.

q: Which account offers tax-free qualified withdrawals in retirement?
r: A Roth IRA
Contributions are made with after-tax money.
w: A traditional IRA whose contributions are deducted and whose withdrawals are taxed
Withdrawals are taxed.
A regular taxable brokerage account where gains are taxed each year as they are earned
Gains are taxed.
A certificate of deposit at a bank whose interest is taxed as ordinary income
Interest is taxed.

q: What is a traditional IRA's main tax feature?
r: Contributions may be tax-deductible and are taxed when withdrawn
Taxes are deferred until retirement.
w: Contributions are made after tax and all withdrawals in retirement are free of tax
That describes a Roth IRA.
Taxes are paid every year on the growth of the account and again at withdrawal
Growth is tax-deferred.
Contributions are limited to wealthy investors who have very high yearly incomes
Many can contribute.

q: Why should most investors read a fund's prospectus before investing?
r: It describes the fund's goals, fees and risks
Investors need these facts to compare funds.
w: It guarantees the fund will earn a profit for investors in the next twelve months
No guarantee exists.
It lists the personal phone numbers of the fund's managers for investors to call
Not its purpose.
It is required to be read only by the staff of the regulator and not by the investors
Investors should read it.

q: What is the best reason to avoid investing based only on a hot tip from social media?
r: Tips may be false, promotional or part of a scheme
Investors should do their own research.
w: Tips are guaranteed by the regulators so they cannot lose money for any investor
No guarantee exists.
Social media posts are always accurate when they come from someone with many followers
Followers do not prove accuracy.
Tips from social media are illegal for investors to read under securities laws
Reading them is legal.

q: What is a limit on diversification when investing in only one sector?
r: A downturn in that sector can hurt the entire portfolio
Risk is concentrated.
w: The sector's stocks always rise together so the portfolio is protected from any loss
They can fall together.
The investor cannot sell any of the shares until the whole sector rises in value
Shares can be sold.
The investor must pay a special tax to the government for holding a single sector
No such tax exists.

q: What does 'past performance does not guarantee future results' mean?
r: Earlier returns do not promise the same returns later
Markets and funds change over time.
w: Past returns will always repeat in the same pattern in each future year without change
They may not repeat.
Funds that did well in the past will be required by law to keep doing well in the future
No law requires that.
Past losses are erased from the record of the fund after a period of three years
Records are kept.

q: What is a good first step before choosing investments?
r: Define your goals, time horizon and risk tolerance
These shape the right mix.
w: Pick the stock that has risen the most this week because many investors are buying it
That is chasing performance.
Borrow as much money as possible so that more can be placed into the market quickly
That raises risk.
Choose the investment with the highest advertised return without reading any details
That ignores risk.

r: The original price paid for an asset, including fees
It is used to compute gains and losses.
w: The current price at which the asset trades on the exchange between buyers and sellers
That is market price.
The price at which the asset will be sold when the investor chooses to leave the market
That is a sale price.
The amount of tax that the investor owes when the asset is sold at a profit
That is a tax amount.

r: Profit from selling an asset for more than its cost
Gains are taxed when realized.
w: Interest paid on a savings account by a bank to its customer at the end of each month
That is interest.
A payment made by a company to its shareholders out of the profits it has earned
That is a dividend.
The amount a broker earns for executing a trade on behalf of a client of the firm
That is a commission.
